Police say the incident involved nationality-based insults and damage to the children’s toy drone. by TVP World | Aug. 19, 2026, 9:00 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A military police officer looks on as Polish border guards check cars at the Polish-German border in Slubice, western Poland, close to the German city of Frankfurt an der Oder, on July 7, 2025, as Poland temporarily reintroduced border controls with Germany and Lithuania, saying they are needed to control “illegal immigration”. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip A Polish woman has been charged over an alleged nationality-based attack on two Ukrainian siblings playing in a park in the northern city of Bydgoszcz. Police received a report that a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother had been subjected to verbal abuse and physical violence by two adults on Friday afternoon. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . On Tuesday, police detained a 46-year-old woman in connection with the case and charged her with nationality-based insults , violating the bodily integrity of a minor and damaging property. A 34-year-old man who was with the woman during the alleged attack was also detained. He was questioned as a witness and has not been charged, Poland’s state news agency PAP reported. Advertisement The incident comes amid concern over anti-Ukrainian hostility in Poland. Poland has been one of Kyiv’s staunchest allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, but anti-Ukrainian sentiment has also grown in recent years, while the countries’ complex shared history continues to cast a shadow over bilateral relations. ‘Anti-Polish act’ Polish police said the incident occurred while the children were playing with a toy drone. “The couple most likely did not like the fact that the children were using a toy drone. It was destroyed. They also allegedly made comments about the children’s nationality,” Monika Chlebicz, a spokeswoman for Bydgoszcz regional police, was quoted as saying by Polish broadcaster TVN24. Other Topics of Interest Russian Strike Halts DTEK Thermal Power Plant One of DTEK’s plants in Ukraine has stopped producing electricity entirely after equipment sustained significant damage in an attack. “According to the information we received, they twisted the 12-year-old boy’s arm,” she said, adding that the children did not require medical treatment. The incident also drew a response from Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk. “Attacking children is an anti-Polish act,” he said ahead of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday. “As Poles, we have always been very proud of the way we treat our children and children who seek refuge in our country,” he added. Advertisement Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also addressed the incident, saying: “Zero tolerance for hatred, especially hatred directed at children.” On Sunday, the Ukrainian Consulate General in Gdańsk, a northern Polish port city, said it was monitoring the case and remained in contact with the children’s mother. “We strongly condemn all manifestations of xenophobia,” it added. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2.text: Image source, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz / Julie Van Collie Image caption, The only known living member of the species is in a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia By Helen Briggs Environment Correspondent Published 18 September 2026, 00:15 BST A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species. The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes. But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals. Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers. Image source, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz / Julie Van Collie Image caption, The cat has been given the nickname Tigrino Tiger cats are small, spotted wild cats found across Central and South America, from Costa Rica to Bolivia and Argentina. They look remarkably similar and even experts can struggle to tell them apart. "It's an amazing result that we have a new species for the world, which is the Leopardus tilcayo ," said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz of Universidad Mayor de San Andres in La Paz, Bolivia. "It's amazing that there are still new species waiting to be discovered: we don't have to go to a volcano, an island, or deep into the sea." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The oncilla, or northern tiger cat, looks remarkably similar Only one confirmed living member of the species is known - a cat in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist. It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery. Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual. It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat. Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists. To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens. "There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. The study, published in Current Biology , external , uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat ( Leopardus tilcayo ) of Bolivia. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bolivia has dense forest that supports thousands of rare plant and animals However, identifying the species is only the first step. Co-researcher Dr Caroline Sartor, of the Wildlife Conservation Research Unit at the University of Oxford, said the discovery was important for conservation because it is impossible to protect a species if we don't know what it is or where it lives. "These are animals similar in size to a domestic cat, so you might think we would know them all by now, but this discovery shows how much biodiversity is still to be uncovered in some of the less-studied regions of the world," she said. Tiger cat species are considered vulnerable to extinction because of deforestation, habitat loss and illegal hunting, although the new species is missing from previous assessments. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The new discovery suggests the world's cat family - all domestic and wild cats, big and small - will expand from 41 known species to 44 or 45 The discovery could also have wider implications for the world's cat family. Both wild and domestic cats belong to the biological family Felidae, which includes every living cat species from tiny house pets to massive tigers. There are officially 41 species recognised but the new discovery, and the finding that there may be several species of tiger cat, brings the number to 44 or more. Andrew Kitchener, an expert in mammals at National Museums, Scotland, who was not involved with the research, says the small spotted South American cats known as tiger cats have been a "taxonomic nightmare". "These cats are confusing because they look so similar and there are few specimens in museums, so even now we are still learning how to tell them apart as genetics reveal more species," he said. https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/us/.text: The Pentagon is considering big changes to how it positions US forces in Europe and the Middle East, in what could amount to a major military shake-up. President Donald Trump's administration made it clear in this year's National Defence Strategy that it wants allies to do more in Europe and the Middle East so the US can focus on China and the Western Hemisphere, where Washington is increasingly targeting drug cartels in South America. In the Gulf, the war in Iran has underscored how vulnerable troops posted to the region can be. At least 18 US service members have been killed, including six in an Iranian missile strike at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. "Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan," an inspector general's report into the costs of the war found. The report, released this week, also said Pentagon officials have yet to decide whether they will return base and troop levels to what they were before the war. The Pentagon "has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs allies partners will contribute", the report states. The Washington Post has reported that the Pentagon is looking at whether it will move troops away from the Gulf. Typically, about 40,000 US personnel are based across the region. An official told the Post that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had not yet ordered a formal review of force posture in the Middle East. CNN on Friday reported that the Pentagon is expected to send MQ-9 Reaper drones currently operating in Africa to be used in South America as the US increases its anti-narcotics operations. Mr Hegseth in June announced a six-month review for Europe that is looking at the US troop presence there. The effort is led by Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defence for policy, who has long advocated greater focus on deterring China. Among the possibilities being considered by Pentagon officials, Reuters reported on Thursday, is ​withdrawing about 25,000 troops from Europe, a move that would worry European and Nato officials who are facing an increasingly confrontational Russia. The US currently has about 80,000 troops in Europe. While reducing force levels in Europe or the Middle East could free up resources for other priorities, it also raises questions about US deterrence in both regions and the reliability of Washington's commitments. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the senior Democrat on the Senate foreign ⁠relations committee, on Thursday asked Secretary of ​State Marco Rubio to ensure that US diplomats are ⁠involved in the Pentagon-led review of America's military presence in Europe. In a letter addressed ​to Mr Rubio, who is also National Security Adviser, Ms Shaheen said that diplomats, including US ambassadors, are being kept out of the loop. "The Department of State, which is responsible for managing our bilateral relationships, has traditionally played a substantial role in reviews of this kind," she said in the letter. "Yet what we are hearing through our own conversations, travel across Europe and engagement with our allies tells a different story. US ambassadors and chiefs of mission in affected countries have been excluded from consultations." A State Department official disputed the issues raised in the letter, saying that diplomats were being consulted. Ms Shaheen wrote that adjustments in troop levels ⁠would have an effect on bilateral relationships that the State Department would be left to manage, with the Baltic nations of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia among the countries with the most at stake. European leaders have warned of incidents, often attributed to Russia, that fall below the threshold of conventional military attacks but undermine European security – such as sabotage, arson and drone incursions.
